name: eip681-conformance-vectors
notes: Each vector lists an input URI and the properties a conforming implementation must produce.
Vectors marked spec:true are taken directly from the EIP-681 text or its examples.
Vectors marked spec:false are real-world failure cases documented in the field; they pin down
behaviour the spec implies but does not spell out.
'canonical' is the deterministically re-serialised form: scheme:target@chainId/function?params
with query parameters in the fixed order address,uint256,value,gas,gasPrice and no trailing '?'.

vectors.why: EIP-681 allows an optional 'pay-' prefix on the target address. A parser that does not strip it will reject a valid URI or compute the wrong recipient hash.
This is canonical EIP-55 vector #1. Mixed case means the checksum is meaningful and valid.

Same address with the final character case flipped. Mixed case is an EIP-55 checksum claim, so this must be rejected rather than silently lowercased. A lax parser here sends funds derived from a malformed address string.
All-lowercase carries no checksum information, so it cannot be wrong. Rejecting it would break every address produced by a tool that lowercases output.

The correct form for publishing a token deposit address: bare address, no /transfer, no amount. A partial parser sees a plain payee and sends a native transfer; that is recoverable by the recipient. The /transfer form is NOT safe to publish publicly because such a parser would read the token contract as the payee.
Valid per grammar, dangerous in practice: the wallet chooses the network, so one QR can be paid on the wrong chain.

value= is the native coin amount, uint256= is the token amount. EIP-681 makes them mutually exclusive and implementations disagree about which wins, so a conforming parser must refuse rather than guess.
uint256= is a contract-call argument. With no /transfer in the path there is no call to carry it, so the amount is unpayable as written.

1e18 wei is 1 ETH. Serialising this through a float gives 1000000000000000000 exactly, but through a JS Number it is not safe for amounts above 2^53. The amount must be carried as a decimal string or bigint.
Exactly 2^256-1 must be accepted; one more must be rejected. This is the boundary most implementations get wrong by using Number.
